- pixl:pixl: Use when delegating or producing PixelLab visual assets, including UI, sprites, animation, tiles, fonts, style consistency, inspection and project integration. Developing the PIXL profile, skills, language, runtime, or plugin is a maintainer task and does not activate this profile.
- pixl:plar: Map a project's code, UI states and references to pixel-art asset requirements; create or update plar.txt and hand a selected asset to PIXL for production.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. - Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. - GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 600000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

# Outline and canvas decision brief

This is both the decision brief for the project owner and the retained visual
observation backing criterion `q_aid_useful` for candidate `x_aid`.

- **Sheet:** `deliverables/outline-scale-comparison.png`
- **Built from:** the supplied `reference.png` and `reference-b.png` bytes only, enlarged
  by integer nearest-neighbour at 1x, 2x, 3x, 4x, 6x and 8x over light, dark and busy
  backgrounds. No content was redrawn or resampled; the accompanying local check
  (`evidence/aid-faithfulness.json`) confirmed all 36 panels and 14,040 opaque source
  pixels enlarge into uniform blocks with no invented colour.
- **Reviewer:** PIXL (agent), viewed in this session, 2026-09-14.
- **Outcome for `q_aid_useful`:** pass, with one stated limit.

## What the sheet shows

**The outline decision is really a background decision.** This is the finding that
matters, and it is not visible in either reference on its own.

- On the **light** band both treatments read well. The unoutlined teal has ample
  contrast against a pale field and needs no help; the outline adds articulation but is
  not doing separation work.
- On the **dark** band the navy outline is close enough in value to the background that
  it partly disappears. The outlined figure reads as a *smaller* teal shape with a soft
  dark fringe, and the top stalks nearly vanish because they are entirely outline
  colour. The unoutlined figure reads more strongly and holds its full size.
- On the **busy** band the relationship inverts. The dark contour is what lifts the
  outlined figure off the noisy mid-value field, while the unoutlined teal begins to
  blend into it, particularly at the smaller scales.

So: if the game's levels are predominantly dark, the outline in `reference.png` actively
costs readability. If the levels are busy or mid-value, the outline is what makes the
character separable. Choosing the outline without knowing the backgrounds risks picking
the treatment that fails where the game actually is.

**The outline costs apparent size.** At 6x and 8x the teal interior of the outlined
figure is visibly smaller than the full teal body of the unoutlined one. The 2 px
contour consumes 180 of 390 visible pixels. On a canvas smaller than the references'
32 x 32, that cost grows proportionally and leaves very little interior in which a scout
and a medic could differ from one another.

**Legibility of the difference by scale.** At 1x the two treatments are not reliably
distinguishable — the figure is 18 x 25 device pixels and the outline reads as a general
darkening rather than as a contour. At 2x the eyes resolve. From 3x upward the outline
treatment is unambiguous. This is the stated limit on the pass: the sheet supports the
decision at 3x and above, and shows that at 1x the decision barely matters visually.

## What this does not decide

The sheet does not choose for you. Per the bundled `edge-rhythm` method, contour style is
authored intent and must not be resolved mechanically, and per `silhouette-readability`,
no contrast ratio or pixel count proves aesthetic quality. Both treatments are viable;
they serve different backgrounds.

## Bearing on the canvas choice

The two decisions are coupled, so it is worth taking them together:

- Keeping the 2 px outline argues for **32 x 32 or larger**, so that interior area
  remains for role differentiation between the scout and the medic.
- Dropping the outline makes a **smaller canvas** viable, because the full canvas is
  available to the figure — but then the shoulder bar, base bar and solid stalks that the
  navy currently carries have to be re-authored as a second teal value or a cream accent,
  or the characters lose those landmarks entirely.

13	`training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-ASSETS.md` lines 11-15.

# Method research for the two open decisions

Retrieved 2026-09-14 from the bundled PIXL knowledge library via `pixl_knowledge`.
These are the library's own words and source locators, recorded so the reasoning behind
this project's criteria is traceable. **A bundled method and its bundled proof-of-concept
receipt are context for this project, not proof about this project's assets.**

## silhouette-readability

Title: "Evaluate identity using silhouette and target backgrounds".
Applies to: characters, inventory icons, interactive props.
Sources: `training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-DEEP-RESEARCH.md` lines 857-867 and 1563-1573;
`training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-ASSETS.md` lines 11-15.

Requires: "Intended viewing scale, representative backgrounds and identity landmarks".
Checks: "Named identity landmarks remain visible at the target size."
Pitfalls the library states explicitly: "Silhouette alone cannot validate faces,
materials or fine symbols." and "No contrast ratio or component count proves aesthetic
quality."

**Applicability here.** This is why the project's readability and role criteria are
declared with domain `visual` and mode `visual`, and why the scout/medic distinction is
stated as an observable landmark condition at native scale rather than as a pixel count.
It also means the outline question cannot be settled by measuring the references: the
library explicitly denies that component counts or contrast decide aesthetics.

## edge-rhythm

Title: "Audit stair-step runs without imposing one contour style".
Sources: `training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-DEEP-RESEARCH.md` lines 1402-1431 and 857-867.

Pitfalls the library states explicitly: "Not every uneven run is a jaggy; shape can
require an abrupt change." and "Mechanical contour smoothing can erase style and
identity."

**Applicability here.** This is the direct reason the outline disagreement is retained
as a conflict for the user rather than resolved by the agent. The library's position is
that contour style is authored intent, so picking one reference over the other is a
style decision belonging to the project owner, not a cleanup the agent should perform.

## integer-presentation

Title: "Render at a declared logical grid and inspect device pixels".
Sources: `training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-DEEP-RESEARCH.md` lines 907-919, 1293-1315,
1636-1638.

Requires: "Logical resolution, camera convention and target viewport dimensions".
Pitfalls: "Nearest filtering alone does not constrain lighting resolution." and
"Noninteger scaling, arbitrary rotation and browser zoom can change displayed pixel
widths."

**Applicability here.** The method requires a target viewport/display scale as an input.
This project has neither a canvas size nor a display scale, which is why the canvas
choice is recorded as unresolved together with a separate unresolved display-scale
choice, and why the engine criterion is declared but cannot be exercised.

## Consequence for this session

None of these methods supplies a value for the two open decisions. They establish that
the decisions are the owner's to make and that they are coupled, which is recorded in
`reference-observations.md`. No method was adopted into a design decision (`D`) this
session, and no proof was executed for one, because production has not been authorized
to start.

   enlargement to 384 x 384 (integer factor 12), and viewed at that size.

At native 32 x 32 the images were legible only as two small coloured blocks; the
outline difference was not reliably judgeable at that size. The integer enlargement is
what made the treatments distinguishable, and the observations below come from it.

- Both figures are the same bilaterally symmetric, front-facing blocky form: a body
  block with two vertical stalks rising from the top, separated by a central notch.
- Two cream rectangles sit side by side in the upper-middle of the body and read
  immediately as eyes. They are taller than they are wide, mirrored about the vertical
  axis, and level with each other. This matches the measured 3-wide x 4-tall clusters at
  x 11..13 and x 18..20, y 14..17.
- **reference.png** shows a flat dark navy border of even thickness running all the way

  horizontal bar across the figure below the stalks, a second bar across the bottom, and

1	# Outline and canvas decision brief
2	
3	This is both the decision brief for the project owner and the retained visual
4	observation backing criterion `q_aid_useful` for candidate `x_aid`.
5	
6	- **Sheet:** `deliverables/outline-scale-comparison.png`
7	- **Built from:** the supplied `reference.png` and `reference-b.png` bytes only, enlarged
8	  by integer nearest-neighbour at 1x, 2x, 3x, 4x, 6x and 8x over light, dark and busy
9	  backgrounds. No content was redrawn or resampled; the accompanying local check
10	  (`evidence/aid-faithfulness.json`) confirmed all 36 panels and 14,040 opaque source
11	  pixels enlarge into uniform blocks with no invented colour.
12	- **Reviewer:** PIXL (agent), viewed in this session, 2026-09-14.
13	- **Outcome for `q_aid_useful`:** pass, with one stated limit.
14	
15	## What the sheet shows
16	
17	**The outline decision is really a background decision.** This is the finding that
18	matters, and it is not visible in either reference on its own.
19	
20	- On the **light** band both treatments read well. The unoutlined teal has ample
21	  contrast against a pale field and needs no help; the outline adds articulation but is
22	  not doing separation work.
23	- On the **dark** band the navy outline is close enough in value to the background that
24	  it partly disappears. The outlined figure reads as a *smaller* teal shape with a soft
25	  dark fringe, and the top stalks nearly vanish because they are entirely outline
26	  colour. The unoutlined figure reads more strongly and holds its full size.
27	- On the **busy** band the relationship inverts. The dark contour is what lifts the
28	  outlined figure off the noisy mid-value field, while the unoutlined teal begins to
29	  blend into it, particularly at the smaller scales.
30	
31	So: if the game's levels are predominantly dark, the outline in `reference.png` actively
32	costs readability. If the levels are busy or mid-value, the outline is what makes the
33	character separable. Choosing the outline without knowing the backgrounds risks picking
34	the treatment that fails where the game actually is.
35	
36	**The outline costs apparent size.** At 6x and 8x the teal interior of the outlined
37	figure is visibly smaller than the full teal body of the unoutlined one. The 2 px
38	contour consumes 180 of 390 visible pixels. On a canvas smaller than the references'
39	32 x 32, that cost grows proportionally and leaves very little interior in which a scout
40	and a medic could differ from one another.
41	
42	**Legibility of the difference by scale.** At 1x the two treatments are not reliably
43	distinguishable — the figure is 18 x 25 device pixels and the outline reads as a general
44	darkening rather than as a contour. At 2x the eyes resolve. From 3x upward the outline
45	treatment is unambiguous. This is the stated limit on the pass: the sheet supports the
46	decision at 3x and above, and shows that at 1x the decision barely matters visually.
47	
48	## What this does not decide
49	
50	The sheet does not choose for you. Per the bundled `edge-rhythm` method, contour style is
51	authored intent and must not be resolved mechanically, and per `silhouette-readability`,
52	no contrast ratio or pixel count proves aesthetic quality. Both treatments are viable;
53	they serve different backgrounds.
54	
55	## Bearing on the canvas choice
56	
57	The two decisions are coupled, so it is worth taking them together:
58	
59	- Keeping the 2 px outline argues for **32 x 32 or larger**, so that interior area
60	  remains for role differentiation between the scout and the medic.
61	- Dropping the outline makes a **smaller canvas** viable, because the full canvas is
62	  available to the figure — but then the shoulder bar, base bar and solid stalks that the
63	  navy currently carries have to be re-authored as a second teal value or a cream accent,
64	  or the characters lose those landmarks entirely.
65

1	# Measured observations of the supplied references
2	
3	Measured 2026-09-14 with the bundled asset check and direct pixel reads, then inspected
4	visually at native scale and at 12x nearest-neighbour enlargement
5	(`work/reference-views/`). Measurements are mechanical; the style judgements below are
6	labelled where they are inference rather than measurement.
7	
8	## Identity
9	
10	| | reference.png | reference-b.png |
11	|---|---|---|
12	| sha256 | d997cade…70aa7 | e76b40ce…14a12a |
13	| canvas | 32 x 32 | 32 x 32 |
14	| visible pixels | 390 | 390 |
15	| visible bbox | x 7..24, y 3..27 (18 x 25) | identical |
16	| visible colours | 3 | 2 |
17	| fractional-alpha pixels | 0 | 0 |
18	| opaque components (4-connectivity) | 1 | 1 |
19	
20	## Shared, measured
21	
22	- Identical alpha mask. Every visible pixel in one is visible in the other.
23	- Binary alpha in both files: zero fractional-alpha pixels.
24	- Body colour `#56B5BC` (teal) and detail colour `#F4DDA2` (cream) in both.
25	- Two cream clusters, each exactly 3 wide x 4 tall: x 11..13 and x 18..20, both y 14..17.
26	  They read as eyes and are mirror-symmetric about the figure's vertical axis.
27	- The figure is bilaterally symmetric and front-facing, with two vertical stalks at the
28	  top separated by a notch.
29	- No anti-aliasing and no dithering in either file.
30	
31	## The outline disagreement, measured
32	
33	The two files differ in exactly 180 pixels, and every one of those differences is the
34	same substitution: `#25354A` (dark navy) in reference.png becomes `#56B5BC` (teal) in
35	reference-b.png. There is no other difference.
36	
37	- **reference.png**: a flat 2-logical-pixel navy outline fully enclosing the teal body.
38	  The two top stalks are 4 px wide and therefore rendered entirely in outline colour,
39	  with no teal interior. Two full-width navy bars at y 9..10 and y 26..27 read as a
40	  shoulder line and a base line. Outline is a single flat colour with no ramp.
41	- **reference-b.png**: no outline. Flat teal silhouette, cream eyes only. The shoulder
42	  and base bars and the stalk interiors disappear entirely, because they were drawn in
43	  the outline colour rather than as separate shapes.
44	
45	**Inference, not measurement:** the outline in reference.png is not decorative trim. It
46	carries interior structure (the shoulder bar, the base bar, and the solidity of the
47	stalks). Dropping it, as reference-b.png does, removes readable landmarks, not just the
48	contour. A decision for the unoutlined treatment therefore has to re-author that
49	interior structure in some other way — a second teal value, or a cream accent — rather
50	than simply deleting the outline colour.
51	
52	## Coupling between outline and canvas size, inference
53	
54	A 2 px outline on an 18 x 25 figure spends roughly 46% of the visible pixels (180 of
55	390) on contour and bars. That ratio is a property of the figure's size, so the outline
56	decision and the canvas decision are not independent:
57	
58	- On a canvas materially smaller than 32 x 32, a 2 px outline would leave very little
59	  interior for a scout/medic to differ in, and the two characters would be hard to tell
60	  apart.
61	- On a canvas materially larger than 32 x 32, a 2 px outline thins out visually and
62	  reads closer to a 1 px line at the reference's apparent weight.
63	
64	## What the references do not establish
65	
66	- **Projection.** Both figures are front-facing and symmetric. Neither shows a side
67	  view, which is the stated destination. The references establish colour, edge language,
68	  alpha behaviour and detail density; they do not establish the side-view silhouette,
69	  limb construction, or a facing direction.
70	- **Scout and medic differentiation.** Neither reference carries role-identifying
71	  equipment or a distinguishing accent colour.
72	- **Target display scale, engine, or importer.**
73	- **Animation poses, cycles, directions or timing.**
74

1	# Method research for the two open decisions
2	
3	Retrieved 2026-09-14 from the bundled PIXL knowledge library via `pixl_knowledge`.
4	These are the library's own words and source locators, recorded so the reasoning behind
5	this project's criteria is traceable. **A bundled method and its bundled proof-of-concept
6	receipt are context for this project, not proof about this project's assets.**
7	
8	## silhouette-readability
9	
10	Title: "Evaluate identity using silhouette and target backgrounds".
11	Applies to: characters, inventory icons, interactive props.
12	Sources: `training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-DEEP-RESEARCH.md` lines 857-867 and 1563-1573;
13	`training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-ASSETS.md` lines 11-15.
14	
15	Requires: "Intended viewing scale, representative backgrounds and identity landmarks".
16	Checks: "Named identity landmarks remain visible at the target size."
17	Pitfalls the library states explicitly: "Silhouette alone cannot validate faces,
18	materials or fine symbols." and "No contrast ratio or component count proves aesthetic
19	quality."
20	
21	**Applicability here.** This is why the project's readability and role criteria are
22	declared with domain `visual` and mode `visual`, and why the scout/medic distinction is
23	stated as an observable landmark condition at native scale rather than as a pixel count.
24	It also means the outline question cannot be settled by measuring the references: the
25	library explicitly denies that component counts or contrast decide aesthetics.
26	
27	## edge-rhythm
28	
29	Title: "Audit stair-step runs without imposing one contour style".
30	Sources: `training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-DEEP-RESEARCH.md` lines 1402-1431 and 857-867.
31	
32	Pitfalls the library states explicitly: "Not every uneven run is a jaggy; shape can
33	require an abrupt change." and "Mechanical contour smoothing can erase style and
34	identity."
35	
36	**Applicability here.** This is the direct reason the outline disagreement is retained
37	as a conflict for the user rather than resolved by the agent. The library's position is
38	that contour style is authored intent, so picking one reference over the other is a
39	style decision belonging to the project owner, not a cleanup the agent should perform.
40	
41	## integer-presentation
42	
43	Title: "Render at a declared logical grid and inspect device pixels".
44	Sources: `training/original-docs/PIXEL-ART-DEEP-RESEARCH.md` lines 907-919, 1293-1315,
45	1636-1638.
46	
47	Requires: "Logical resolution, camera convention and target viewport dimensions".
48	Pitfalls: "Nearest filtering alone does not constrain lighting resolution." and
49	"Noninteger scaling, arbitrary rotation and browser zoom can change displayed pixel
50	widths."
51	
52	**Applicability here.** The method requires a target viewport/display scale as an input.
53	This project has neither a canvas size nor a display scale, which is why the canvas
54	choice is recorded as unresolved together with a separate unresolved display-scale
55	choice, and why the engine criterion is declared but cannot be exercised.
56	
57	## Consequence for this session
58	
59	None of these methods supplies a value for the two open decisions. They establish that
60	the decisions are the owner's to make and that they are coupled, which is recorded in
61	`reference-observations.md`. No method was adopted into a design decision (`D`) this
62	session, and no proof was executed for one, because production has not been authorized
63	to start.
64

23	
24	- Both figures are the same bilaterally symmetric, front-facing blocky form: a body
25	  block with two vertical stalks rising from the top, separated by a central notch.
26	- Two cream rectangles sit side by side in the upper-middle of the body and read

31	  around the teal body, with no gradient or ramp within it. The same navy also forms a

36	  the two cream eyes. The horizontal bars and the dark stalks are absent, and the stalks

38	  and less articulated than reference.png, and loses the shoulder and base landmarks

46	The description of the outline treatment and of eye placement in

52	
53	This receipt covers only the supplied reference art. It establishes no acceptance for

intake.rationale: Both references contain zero fractional-alpha pixels. Observed from the source art; not yet confirmed as this project output policy.

The predominant level backgrounds of the side-view game are not stated. The retained comparison sheet showed the navy outline separates the figure on busy mid-value backgrounds but nearly disappears on dark ones, so the outline decision depends on this. The light, dark and busy bands used in the readability criterion are the agent's test set, not the game's backgrounds.

The user has explicitly not chosen the final canvas size. Both references are 32x32 carrying an 18x25 figure, which is an observation about the source art and not an adopted project value. This choice blocks every raster output plan.

intake.value: Carry the flat colour, absent anti-aliasing, binary alpha and blocky low-detail construction of the references into a genuinely side-view figure; treat the front-facing symmetric shape of the references as a style swatch rather than as the character design.
intake.rationale: Proposal needing the agreement of the owner. Both references are front-facing and bilaterally symmetric while the stated destination is a side-view game, so the reference pose cannot be reproduced literally. This proposal states which parts of the references are being matched and which are not.

The target on-screen integer zoom is not stated. The bundled integer-presentation method requires a target viewport as an input, and the scale bounds how much interior detail survives, so it interacts with the canvas choice.
No destination engine or importer is named, so no engine import acceptance can be performed in this project yet.

value: reference.png: flat 2px dark outline #25354A fully enclosing the body, also carrying the shoulder bar, base bar and solid top stalks
reference-b.png: no outline, flat teal silhouette with cream eyes only
intake.rationale: The user states the references disagree here. Measured: the two files differ in exactly 180 pixels and every difference is #25354A becoming #56B5BC. The outline is load-bearing rather than trim, because removing it also removes the shoulder bar, base bar and stalk interiors. Retained as a conflict; the bundled edge-rhythm method states contour style is authored intent and must not be resolved mechanically.

Measured from the references: teal body, cream eyes, and navy present only in reference.png. Observed, not agreed. Whether #25354A belongs to the output palette depends entirely on the unresolved outline decision, so this cannot be confirmed first.

How a scout reads as a scout and a medic as a medic is not stated, and neither reference carries role-identifying equipment or accent colour. At the detail density of the references this needs a deliberate device, such as a reserved accent hue or a silhouette attachment.
The brief names exactly these two family members.
Proposal. Neither reference contains anti-aliasing or dithering, so nearest sampling preserves the supplied look. Proposed rather than confirmed because the display scale and engine are unknown.
The brief states the destination is a side-view game.
